titles: What Happens to AI If the Leather Jacket Leaves?
The Man, the Jacket, and the AI Chip Empire

beats.vo: One man in a leather jacket runs AI hardware.
beats.visual: Noir miniature city at night, rain on tiny streets. A single spotlight hits a glossy black leather jacket on a hanger, floating above a skyline made of circuit boards. Faint synth hum.

beats.vo: His name is Jensen Huang, and he has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993.
beats.visual: Claymation flashback in sepia: a small clay figure in a modest diner booth sketching chip diagrams on a napkin. A wall calendar flips to 1993. The napkin sketch glows green.

beats.vo: Nvidia designs the chips that a lot of the biggest AI models are trained on.
beats.visual: Paper diorama data center: endless rows of cardboard server racks, each with a tiny green Nvidia-style glowing chip. Paper robots, chatbots and image generators line up to plug in.

beats.vo: So when people wonder if he might step down, the whole tech economy leans in.
beats.visual: A miniature stock exchange floor where clay traders all freeze and tilt toward the empty leather jacket at the same angle, like a field of sunflowers turning to the sun.

beats.vo: Some people even put real money on it, trading bets on prediction markets like Polymarket.
beats.visual: A smoky noir card table. Tiny hands push poker chips stamped YES and NO toward a placard reading LEAVES BY 2026? A ticker of moving prices crawls across the felt.

beats.vo: But here is the twist. Nvidia does not manufacture its own chips.
beats.visual: Record scratch. The camera whips out of the casino window and across a paper ocean. The jacket on its hanger spins slowly, looking almost embarrassed.

beats.vo: It designs them. A company called TSMC, in Taiwan, builds them.
beats.visual: Macro miniature fab in Taiwan: workers in white clean-room suits move wafers under yellow light. CAMEO: the curious penguin in a tiny bunny suit waddles past carrying a single wafer, stops, stares at camera, keeps walking.

beats.vo: And the real moat is software. CUDA, a toolkit developers have used for years, is built for Nvidia hardware.
beats.visual: Surreal landscape: a medieval castle made of green chips, surrounded by a glowing moat of flowing code. Little developer figures sit on the drawbridge with laptops, fishing lines dangling into the code.

beats.vo: Switching chips can mean rewriting a lot of code. Most companies would rather not.
beats.visual: A tiny clay developer stares at a mountain of printed code pages taller than a building, sighs, and quietly sits back down on the drawbridge.

beats.vo: So if he left, the chips would keep shipping and the code would keep running.
beats.visual: Wide shot: paper cargo ships leave the Taiwan fab, server lights blink on across the cardboard data center, robots keep humming. Nothing stops.

beats.vo: The revolution would be fine. The jacket, though, has no clear successor.
beats.visual: Back to the noir spotlight. The leather jacket hangs alone. The penguin waddles in, tries it on, completely swallowed by it, only the beak poking out of the collar. Cut to black.

script.vo: One man in a leather jacket runs AI hardware. His name is Jensen Huang, and he has run Nvidia since he co-founded it in 1993. Nvidia designs the chips that a lot of the biggest AI models are trained on. So when people wonder if he might step down, the whole tech economy leans in. Some people even put real money on it, trading bets on prediction markets like Polymarket. But here is the twist. Nvidia does not manufacture its own chips. It designs them. A company called TSMC, in Taiwan, builds them. And the real moat is software. CUDA, a toolkit developers have used for years, is built for Nvidia hardware. Switching chips can mean rewriting a lot of code. Most companies would rather not. So if he left, the chips would keep shipping and the code would keep running. The revolution would be fine. The jacket, though, has no clear successor.
verify: Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has served as CEO since its founding
Nvidia is fabless and its leading AI chips are manufactured by TSMC in Taiwan
A large share of major AI models are trained on Nvidia GPUs (keep wording general, avoid a specific market share figure unless sourced)
CUDA is Nvidia's proprietary platform designed for Nvidia GPUs and is widely used by AI developers
Polymarket currently lists an active market on whether Jensen Huang leaves Nvidia by 2026 (confirm market wording and that it is still open before publishing)
Avoid referencing the unverified personal allegations in the trending YouTube title; they are not used in this script

qc.verdict: The video establishes a charming, intricate wooden aesthetic that effectively supports the metaphorical narrative. Unfortunately, the execution is severely undermined by pervasive AI artifacts, including morphing objects, warped anatomy, and mechanical interactions that defy basic physics.
weak: s02: The wooden microchips morph and change shape as they slide along the track, and the gear teeth do not mesh correctly.
s04: The coins falling onto the scale materialize out of thin air with no visible source.
s07: The mechanical chisel moves up and down but does not actually carve or alter the wooden blocks passing underneath.
s08: The hand drawing the blueprint has distorted, morphing fingers.
s13: The penguin's jump defies gravity (too floaty), and its legs melt into the wood shavings upon landing.
